lessons.title: Design one small, fast test
body: Positive feedback is not the same as validated demand. Before you spend real time building anything, it's worth knowing exactly how far each kind of response actually goes.

Four levels of evidence, from weakest to strongest
General interest — “That sounds interesting,” “I'd definitely use something like that,” “Great idea!” These show curiosity, not willingness to buy. Engagement — following you, commenting on a post, downloading a free resource, joining a free waitlist. Real interest, but still no indication anyone will pay. Meaningful buying intent — asking specific questions about purchasing, requesting checkout details, making a concrete purchase commitment, agreeing to a clearly defined paid preorder. Actual purchase — someone pays the proposed price under clearly disclosed terms. These four are not equally strong evidence, and treating them as if they were is the single most common validation mistake: a compliment, a like and a poll vote all feel encouraging, but none of them is proof anyone will hand over money. An actual payment is stronger evidence than any amount of verbal enthusiasm.

Why this happens before you build
Building first and testing later risks spending weeks creating something nobody wants, adding features customers never needed, targeting the wrong audience, pricing it wrong, or discovering too late that the product is too complicated or poorly positioned. A small test run now can surface any of these problems before the real development work begins — while they're still cheap to fix. You've already completed Modules 1–7: a target customer, a Problem Inventory, a desired outcome, an offer concept, a core deliverable and bonuses, a promise, a unique value proposition, a proposed price, and a product name and positioning. Test that actual offer — not a vaguer idea of it.

Step 1 — Define exactly what you're testing
Before contacting anyone, write down who the offer is for, what problem it solves, what outcome it helps achieve, what's included, your unique value proposition from Module 5, and the proposed price. A vague concept produces vague feedback — “what do you think of a content planning thing” tells you nothing useful back. Present the same core offer and price to everyone you test it on, so the responses can actually be compared to each other. If you change the offer substantially partway through, record that change — otherwise you're comparing reactions to two different offers as if they were one test.

Step 2 — Select 3–5 suitable prospects
Start small — roughly 3–5 people is a practical first test, not a statistically representative sample. Choose people who match the target customer from Module 1, actually experience the problem from Module 2, have a plausible reason to want the outcome, aren't simply friends inclined to encourage you, and can realistically make the purchasing decision themselves. Five genuinely relevant people are worth more here than fifty random contacts — the quality of who you ask matters more than the quantity.

Step 3 — Define what counts as a yes, before you start
This is the step beginners skip, and it's the one that matters most.
WEAK CRITERION
“At least three people say they like the idea.” — measures positive feedback, not willingness to buy.
STRONGER CRITERION
“At least two qualified prospects agree to purchase at the stated price under clearly disclosed preorder terms” — or “at least two qualified prospects make a documented, specific purchasing commitment with a clear next action and deadline.”
A verbal promise is weaker than an actual payment and shouldn't be reported as a sale. Whatever you choose, your criterion needs to be specific, observable, relevant to actually purchasing, and set before you start — not adjusted afterward to match whatever happened. This lesson isn't handing you a universal conversion rate; two out of five isn't a scientifically validated threshold, it's one example of a small, directional test.

Step 4 — Set a deadline
Without a deadline, a validation test quietly turns into indefinite waiting — and an easy excuse to keep moving the goalposts until some response finally counts as a win. Set a start date, an outreach period, a response deadline, a follow-up date, and a decision date. A short, practical window — five to seven days, say — works well as a starting point; it's illustrative, not a universal rule. The deadline's real job is forcing an honest decision on schedule, instead of an indefinite one.

Step 5 — Prepare the offer presentation
You don't need a finished website, a complete product or an expensive funnel. You need to communicate seven things clearly: who it's for, what problem it addresses, what outcome it helps achieve, what's included, the proposed price, what stage the product is actually at right now, and what commitment you're asking for. Being honest about the development stage is not optional — never let a prospect believe an unfinished product is already complete.

Finding people to test this on — if you already have an audience
Existing customers, email subscribers, relevant social media followers, community members, people who previously asked about this topic, and people who engaged with relevant educational content are all worth considering. But don't assume every follower is a qualified prospect — check each one against the target customer from Module 1 before counting them.

Finding people to test this on — if you have no audience yet
Go back to the research venues from Module 1 — Threads, Reddit and relevant subreddits, Facebook Groups, X/Twitter, YouTube comments, Quora, niche forums, relevant Discord communities, relevant professional communities — and look for people already discussing the problem out loud. A hypothetical creator developing a social-media content planning product might look for small business owners publicly discussing running out of content ideas, difficulty posting consistently, spending too much time creating posts, or struggling to plan a content calendar. Module 1 told you where this audience already talks; Module 8 uses those same venues to find specific people for a real offer test. Participate appropriately and approach people individually where that's the norm in the space. Respect each community's rules, don't spam, don't post unsolicited promotions where they're prohibited, don't scrape private data, don't misrepresent why you're reaching out, and always give people an easy, pressure-free way to decline.

What to actually say — a personalised message
Hi [Name], I noticed your post about [specific problem]. I'm developing a [product type] designed to help [target audience] achieve [desired outcome]. It includes [brief explanation of the core deliverable]. I'm currently testing the offer before building the full product. The proposed price is [price]. Would you be open to taking a look and telling me whether this is something you would genuinely consider purchasing? No pressure if it's not relevant to you.
This works because it references the person's actual problem, explains the product clearly, discloses the development stage honestly, states the real price, invites an honest answer, and applies no pressure.

For an existing audience — an announcement
If you're posting to people who already know you, cover the same ground in your own voice: the problem, the proposed solution, who it's for, what's included, the proposed price, and exactly how an interested person takes the next step. No exaggerated claims — the same honesty rules apply whether you're messaging one stranger or announcing to a thousand followers.
A follow-up
One polite follow-up is reasonable if someone hasn't responded. Don't message repeatedly, and respect a clear no the first time it's given — a prospect who feels pressured tells you less, not more, about whether they'd actually buy.

Handling preorders and payment
Testing interest without payment is useful for early conversations and discovery, but it's not proof anyone will actually pay. A paid preorder — the customer pays before the complete product is delivered — is much stronger evidence, but only if you're transparent that the product is still being developed. Before accepting one, disclose clearly: what currently exists, what isn't built yet, exactly what the buyer will receive, the expected delivery date, the price and payment terms, the refund and cancellation conditions, and what happens if you don't deliver as described. A deposit or reservation can indicate genuine commitment if the terms are clear and the commitment is real — but an informal, non-binding expression of interest is not the same thing as payment, and shouldn't be treated as if it were.

Safeguards that are never optional
  • Never pretend an unfinished product already exists.
  • Never invent testimonials or customer results.
  • Never create fake scarcity.
  • Never misrepresent demand.
  • Never hide preorder terms.
  • Never take money without a realistic ability to deliver on the commitment.
  • Never ignore applicable consumer-protection, payment or refund requirements.
If you're not ready to handle money responsibly yet, test through conversations and documented purchase intent first — but go in knowing that's weaker evidence than an actual purchase, not an equivalent substitute for one.

Interpreting what happens next
If people say yes
Record who committed, exactly what they committed to, whether money actually changed hands, whether they accepted the stated price, any conditions attached, and whether the commitment was ever completed. A verbal yes is not the same as a completed transaction — keep that distinction explicit in your own notes. If there's genuine paid demand, you can consider moving ahead with a minimum viable version you can responsibly deliver. A small test is still a small test, though — it doesn't guarantee broader market demand, it just gives you real evidence instead of a guess.
If people say no
Treat it as information, not a personal verdict. The reason usually falls into one of a few buckets: wrong audience, the problem wasn't urgent enough, the outcome wasn't attractive, the price felt too high, the offer wasn't clear enough, a lack of trust, a good-enough existing alternative, bad timing, or an unsuitable format. A respectful follow-up — “Thanks for being honest. Could you share what made this offer unsuitable for you?” — often surfaces which one it was. Don't pressure anyone to justify a no, and be honest with yourself about the difference between gathering useful feedback and trying to talk someone into changing their answer.
If people are interested but don't commit
This is one of the most common outcomes, and it's tempting to count it as a win — don't. Dig into what specifically interested them, what stopped them from committing, whether price was the real issue, whether the offer was unclear, whether they lacked urgency, or whether they already prefer another solution. Interest on its own is not validation, however encouraging it feels.
If nobody responds
Silence usually means the wrong channel, bad timing, a weak message, an inactive community, or poorly chosen prospects — review your outreach itself before concluding the product has no demand at all. Silence is not the same as rejection; it just hasn't told you anything yet.

Deciding what to do next
  • Proceed — meaningful buying evidence from relevant prospects, and you can responsibly deliver on it.
  • Refine — people recognise the problem, but raise specific concerns about the outcome, offer, price or trust.
  • Reconsider — repeated evidence that the problem isn't important enough, the market is unsuitable, or the offer doesn't address what people actually need.
  • Retest — the test itself was too small, poorly targeted or badly run to support a real decision either way.
There's no universal numerical pass/fail line here — you have to weigh the quality of the evidence and the context it came from, not just count yeses.

A complete worked example — hypothetical
The 7-Day Content Planner: a practical content planning toolkit for small business owners who want to organise a week of social media posts through a structured planning workflow, editable templates and guided exercises, at a hypothetical proposed price of $29.
THE TEST
Identify five relevant small business owners, found through public discussions and existing contacts. Present the same offer and price to all five. Clearly explain the full product isn't complete yet. Only offer a preorder if it can genuinely be fulfilled. Set a five-to-seven-day window. Record what actually happens, not impressions.
Five hypothetical responses, and what each one does and doesn't prove:
  • One person says the idea sounds great but doesn't buy — general interest, not evidence of a sale.
  • One person asks for more information — engaged, but still undecided; worth a clarifying follow-up, not yet a yes.
  • One person says the price is too high — useful, specific feedback about the price itself, not necessarily about the offer overall.
  • One person declines because they already use another tool — reveals a real competing alternative, worth noting for Module 5's research.
  • One person completes a paid preorder under clearly disclosed terms — the one response that counts as actual evidence of willingness to pay.
These are hypothetical illustrations, not real market findings or actual customer quotations. With one paid preorder out of five and no other firm commitments, a “at least two qualified prospects” criterion wouldn't be met — this looks more like Refine than Proceed: real interest exists, the price objection and the competing-tool objection are both specific enough to act on, and a second, better-targeted round makes more sense than concluding the idea is dead or rushing to build the full product on one preorder alone.

The last check before you build
Every module before this one produced a reasoned plan. This one produces evidence. That's the entire point of Offer Engineering ending here, not earlier — a well-designed offer is still a guess until a real person has been asked to pay for it and has actually responded.
lessons.insight: A test that only asks for interest, not money or a firm commitment, isn't validation — it's a poll.

exercise.instructions: Name who you'll test this on, what counts as a real yes, and set a deadline.

prompt.title: Validation Prompt
prompt.purpose: Use this to design a fast, real test before you build anything.
prompt.template: You are a lean-validation coach helping someone test an offer before building it. My target customer: {{m1.topMarket}}. My finished offer, name, and price: {{m4.coreDeliverable}} / {{m7.topName}} / {{m6.price}}. Design one small, fast test I could run this week to see if real people will pay for this, without building the full product first. If I haven't told you how I'd actually reach potential customers — an audience, a network, a channel — ask me that before designing the test. If my plan assumes people will pay before I've actually asked for money, call that out: a real validation test asks for a yes with money or a firm commitment attached, not just interest. Return four steps: (1) who you'll approach and how, (2) a short message I could actually send them, (3) what result counts as a real "yes," and (4) a specific deadline for finishing outreach and deciding what the results mean. Once I report back what actually happened, help me interpret it: tell me which responses count as real evidence versus which are just interest, flag any assumption I'm making about what a response means, and recommend whether to proceed, refine, reconsider or retest — don't tell me a small test proves broader market demand either way. Don't invent conversion-rate benchmarks or research about what "usually" validates an offer — design the test and any interpretation from what I've told you about my own situation only.
